Chapter 41 — RAGAS In Depth RAGAS (Retrieval-Augmented Generation Assessment) is the most widely adopted open-source RAG evaluation library. Its core contribution is a family of reference-light, LLM-judged metrics computed from the quadruple (question, contexts, answer, ground truth), each targeting a specific pipeline component. The metric family • Faithfulness: claim decomposition plus per-claim entailment against contexts (Chapter 26 mechanics). • Answer relevancy: reverse-question generation and embedding similarity (Chapter 27). • Context precision / recall: judge-assessed context usefulness and reference coverage (Chapter 28). • Answer correctness: weighted blend of factual overlap with the ground truth (claim-level TP/FP/FN) and semantic similarity. • Extensions: noise sensitivity, multimodal faithfulness, and aspect-critique judges for custom criteria. Strengths and limits Strengths: component attribution out of the box, synthetic test-set generation integrated, framework- agnostic data schema, and large community familiarity that makes scores communicable. Limits: every headline metric is judge-dependent, so all of Chapter 36–37 applies — default prompts are generic and need domain calibration; answer correctness inherits single-reference bias; reverse-question relevancy is embedding-sensitive; and version-to-version metric definitions have shifted, so pin versions and record them in reports. Adoption protocol Start with faithfulness + context recall on a few hundred items; calibrate both against human labels on your domain before trusting thresholds. Use the synthetic generator for breadth but keep a human- curated core for gates. Wrap judge calls with your own logging (prompt hash, model, tokens) — cost surprises are common at scale because each metric makes multiple LLM calls per item. Practical guidance • Treat RAGAS scores as calibrated instruments, not universal constants: thresholds from blog posts rarely transfer to your domain. • Pin the library

Chapter 50 — Public RAG Benchmarks and Benchmark Suites Beyond individual QA datasets (Chapters 53–62), integrated benchmark suites evaluate RAG systems end-to-end under controlled conditions. They answer different questions than component benchmarks and come with distinctive validity traps. What suites offer • Controlled corpora: fixed document collections with known answers, enabling reproducible cross-system comparison — RAGBench-style suites span domains (legal, finance, support) with labeled context relevance and utilization. • Difficulty stratification: single-hop, multi-hop, aggregation, and unanswerable categories with per-category reporting. • Standardized protocols: fixed k, fixed context budgets, prescribed metrics — removing the configuration freedom that makes private comparisons incomparable. • Leaderboards: community reference points for sanity-checking your system's absolute level. Validity traps Contamination: public benchmark questions and answers are in every foundation model's training data; strong closed-book performance inflates apparent RAG quality. Always run the closed-book arm (no retrieval) and report the retrieval lift, not the absolute score. Corpus mismatch: benchmark corpora are clean, English-heavy, and well-structured; your PDFs are none of those. Metric gaming: suites that score only final answers cannot distinguish grounded from memorized correctness — prefer suites with faithfulness/utilization labels. Staleness: static suites stop discriminating as systems saturate them; track whether your suite still has headroom. Practical guidance • Use public suites for sanity checks and paper comparisons; make release decisions on private, domain-matched sets. • Always publish the closed-book baseline alongside RAG scores — the lift is the honest number. • Contribute your hardest sanitized cases back to community suites; saturated benchmarks help nobody. Chapter 86 — Shadow Deployment and Canary Evaluation Between offline gates and full A/B exposure lie two risk-reducing stages: shadow deployment (candidate runs on live traffic, outputs discarded) and canary release (candidate serves a small traffic slice under close watch). Together they catch what offline suites miss without betting the user base. Shadow deployment Mirror live queries to the candidate asynchronously; log its full traces; compare against the incumbent's served answers. Analysis: judge-scored paired comparison on the shadow stream, retrieval delta analysis, latency/cost profiling under real load, and failure-cluster mining. Shadow catches distribution- shift failures (query types absent from test sets), load-dependent bugs, and integration issues — at zero user risk. Budget: shadow doubles inference cost while running; sample rather than mirror everything at scale. Canary release Serve the candidate to 1–5% of traffic with automated rollback triggers: safety-incident rate, error rate, latency p95, and a fast online quality proxy (reformulation spike, thumbs-down ratio versus concurrent incumbent). Ramp in stages (1% → 5% → 25% → 100%) with dwell time at each stage sized to accumulate signal — sparse feedback means 1% canaries need days, not hours, for quality confidence; keep safety triggers instantaneous regardless. Practical guidance • Shadow every model-version change — provider updates are the most common source of silent regressions. • Define rollback triggers before launch, with owners and runbooks; a canary without an automatic kill switch is just a slow outage. • Compare canary cohorts against concurrent incumbent traffic, not historical baselines — traffic mix drifts. Chapter 1 — What RAG Evaluation Is and Why It Matters Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) evaluation is the systematic measurement of how well a system retrieves relevant evidence and uses it to produce correct, grounded answers. Unlike evaluating a standalone language model, RAG evaluation must assess two coupled subsystems — a retriever and a generator — plus the interaction between them. A perfect generator cannot rescue missing evidence, and a perfect retriever cannot rescue a model that ignores its context. The three measurement layers Every RAG evaluation program operates on three layers. Retrieval quality asks whether the right documents appear in the context window, measured with ranking metrics such as recall@k and nDCG. Generation quality asks whether the answer is faithful to the retrieved evidence, relevant to the question, and complete. End-to-end quality asks whether the user's actual task succeeds, which may tolerate imperfect intermediate steps. Layer confusion is the most common evaluation mistake: teams report high answer accuracy while retrieval silently degrades, or optimize retrieval scores that never translate into better answers. Why it is hard • Compound errors: failures multiply across stages, so end-to-end scores hide which component broke. • Open-ended outputs: many phrasings are correct, making exact-match scoring unreliable. • Moving corpora: documents change, so yesterday's golden answers become stale. • Judge dependence: LLM-based scoring introduces its own biases and drift. Practical guidance • Define the user task first; derive metrics from it, not from what is easy to compute. • Instrument every stage so a bad answer can be traced to retrieval, generation, or the prompt. • Treat evaluation as a continuous engineering discipline with owned datasets, budgets, and regression gates — not a one-time benchmark run. Chapter 26 — Faithfulness and Groundedness Faithfulness measures whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context. It is the defining metric of RAG generation quality: the entire architectural premise is that answers come from evidence, and faithfulness is the direct test of that premise. Faithfulness = supported claims / total claims. Decomposition quality dominates measurement quality: merged claims ("X was founded in 1998 and is based in Oslo") hide partial support, and over-splitting inflates denominators with trivial claims. Audit decompositions manually on a sample before trusting the score. What faithfulness does not capture • Correctness: an answer can be perfectly faithful to wrong or outdated context.
